title: Gentle Voice Start
learningGoals: Compare an easy onset with added push
Carry the experience into a phrase

sections.heading: Welcome and what we will explore
sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Gentle Voice Start. A word beginning with a vowel feels as though you switch the voice on with an extra push.

We will recognise the beginning of voicing, compare an easy onset with added push, and carry the experience into a phrase. First I will explain the distinction. Then you will see and hear a demonstration, try a few short phrases, and notice your own experience. We will finish with a short prepared rehearsal and an everyday next step. You can pause or ask a question at any point. A small comfortable experiment is enough.

sections.heading: What this tool means
sections.narration:
Voice onset is the beginning of voiced sound. A gentle start explores a gradual beginning without added force. It is different from using the maximum amount of breath or changing lip contact. The voice can become ordinary and clear after its beginning; persistent breathiness is not a target.

Voice onset is the moment sound begins. We will explore allowing it to start gradually rather than switching it on with an extra push. This differs from the movement of air and the contact of lips or tongue, although they work together. Start with a comfortable sound and carry the experience into a short phrase.

Notice the distinction: The task concerns how sound begins at a comfortable pitch and volume. A forced whisper or pitch change is a different task. You are choosing one feature for this learning experience, rather than inspecting every aspect of speech. We will use short familiar messages so there is room to notice that feature.

sections.heading: Watch and listen
sections.narration:
Watch the demonstration before trying. We will use this message: I have an idea. First listen to the models and notice the feature being compared. The labels on screen identify each version. You can replay either model without copying an uncomfortable contrast.

Now listen once more for the message itself. Whether onset felt comfortable and whether you added pressure to achieve it. This is an invitation to compare your experience, not a demand to match the model exactly. When you are ready, move to a short guided attempt.

visual.altText: Demonstrate gentle onset on a vowel at comfortable pitch and loudness, then a vowel-initial word. Use a soft rising waveform; not a breath-volume target. No forced whisper, added H before every word or persistent breathy voice. Optional hum-to-vowel variation can help explore easy voicing.

sections.heading: Try the three small steps
sections.narration:
Let us try this in small steps. First: Listen to the onset contrast before trying. Next: Try a short comfortable vowel with a gradual voice start. Then: Use a short familiar word and then a phrase.

Use these familiar phrases one at a time: I have an idea. Are we meeting today? It is good to see you. Stop between attempts when you want to. You can listen to a model again, record a short attempt, or leave this part to return later. Keep attention on this one chosen feature; you do not need to check every sound. If the attempt becomes effortful, stop and return to comfortable ordinary speaking.

sections.heading: Compare and check
sections.narration:
Consider what this tool is asking you to explore. What are we exploring at voice onset? You can select an answer and read or hear the explanation. It is a check of the idea, not a test of how you sound.

After the check, notice one observation from your attempt: Whether onset felt comfortable and whether you added pressure to achieve it. It is possible for a movement to feel different while the message still takes effort, or for you to be unsure what changed. You can record that uncertainty without repeating until you obtain a preferred result.

sections.heading: From a phrase to your own message
sections.narration:
Choose a short message you actually want to share. You might use one of the phrases we have practised and add one useful detail in your own words. Give yourself one small cue from the demonstration, then let the message continue. There is no need to increase the amount of the technique to make the attempt count.

After speaking, ask what you noticed about the chosen feature and about the message. You can keep a small useful change, adjust it, or leave the result open. Try another short message only if it serves your learning today.

sections.heading: Your observation and next step
sections.narration:
Before finishing, save one observation. Here is the feature we explored: Whether onset felt comfortable and whether you added pressure to achieve it. Something may have changed, things may have felt much the same, or you may be unsure. Your observation belongs to this attempt and setting.

In focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one feature. In conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; it does not need to become a checklist you monitor throughout the exchange.

Choose one manageable situation in which you would like to speak. You can plan a small practice, have a conversation, revisit the demonstration, or finish here. Save what you would keep, change or leave open.
